section_summary: This section documents the intense debate between the U.S. State Department, the Department of the Army, SCAP headquarters, and the Japanese Government over the reorganization and centralization of Japan's police system in 1948 and 1949. Facing acute municipal financial distress, communist labor unrest, railway sabotage, and incidents such as the Taira station seizure and Mitaka disaster, Prime Minister Shigeru Yoshida and his Cabinet repeatedly pressed for expanded national police authority, mobile reserves, and direct Cabinet control over law enforcement. General Douglas MacArthur and SCAP's Government Section firmly resisted major recentralization as contrary to democratic occupation reforms, defending civilian public safety commissions and local police autonomy while authorizing handgun shipments and minor administrative revisions.

subfiles.about: Argues that moderate police centralization is warranted by public opinion and NSC 13/2 while stressing democratic police training and civil liberties.
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.summary: Argues that moderate police centralization aligns with Japanese public opinion and NSC 13/2, emphasizing democratic education, civil liberties, and internal security without reliance on U.S. forces.
subfiles.title: Draft State-Army Message on Japanese Police Decentralization and Internal Security

subfiles.about: Transmits basic principles under NSC 13/2 to CINCFE regarding mobile national police reserves, an internal security agency, and expanded national police powers.
subfiles.from: Department of the Army, Civil Affairs Division (General Hermon O. Eberle)
subfiles.summary: Furnishes CINCFE basic principles under NSC 13/2 for anticipated Japanese police legislation, proposing a mobile national police reserve, a national internal security agency like the FBI, broadened national police powers, and shipment of .38-caliber revolvers.
subfiles.title: Department of the Army Outgoing Message WAR 92991 to CINCFE on Principles Basic to Japanese Internal Security

subfiles.about: Evaluates SCAP's limited implementation of State Department principles for police strengthening and analyzes equipment, budget, and organizational obstacles.
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Research for Far East
subfiles.summary: This intelligence report assesses SCAP's reluctance to implement NSC 13/2 recommendations for strengthening Japan's police force. It highlights critical equipment shortages, severe budget reductions forcing smaller localities to rely on corrupting private contributions, and SCAP's rejection of Japanese proposals for a 25,000-man national police increase. While the Japanese Government broadened Imperial Ordinance 101 and empowered the Special Investigation Bureau against extremists, plans to reamalgamate small municipal police into the National Rural Police remain deadlocked by SCAP's insistence on decentralization.
subfiles.title: The Status of Police Reorganization in Japan (DRF-137)

subfiles.about: Transmits a memorandum by Vice Consul Richard H. Lamb regarding police organization, jurisdiction, and financial issues in Odawara.
subfiles.from: Cloyce K. Huston, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, USPOLAD, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Transmits Vice Consul Lamb's memorandum on police problems in Odawara, endorsing the recommendation to consult local opinion before reorganization.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 295: Japanese Police Organization in Odawara and Vicinity

subfiles.about: Reports on an interview with Odawara police official Moruji Nakano regarding municipal and rural police relations, local financing difficulties, and proposed district consolidations.
subfiles.from: Richard H. Lamb, Vice Consul, American Consulate General, Yokohama
subfiles.summary: Details discussions with Odawara police official Moruji Nakano regarding jurisdiction, rural-urban police rivalries, and financial distress in small fishing communities like Manazuru, recommending district-level police consolidations and consultation with local communities.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese Police Organization in Odawara and Vicinity

subfiles.about: Reports on a resolution by prefectural governors of Hokkaido and Tohoku requesting the abolition of local autonomous police due to financial distress and rising crime.
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Reports that Hokkaido and Tohoku prefectural governors passed a resolution urging the abolition of autonomous local police due to heavy financial burdens, peak crime rates, and widespread railway sabotage.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Airgram A-194 on Governors' Resolution to Abolish Local Autonomous Police

subfiles.about: Highlights FBIB intercepts of Minister Higai's remarks on police equipment and ratio revision and reports Labor Division Chief Hepler's impending resignation.
subfiles.from: Niles W. Bond and Marshall Green, Division of Northeast Asian Affairs
subfiles.summary: Reviews FBIB reports on Minister Higai's police revision proposals and Hepler's resignation from SCAP's Labor Division.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on FBIB Reports Concerning Police Revision and SCAP Labor Division
subfiles.to: John M. Allison, Office of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Transmits an interview with State Minister Senzo Higai stressing the need to improve police mobility and adjust the ratio between national and local police.
subfiles.from: James Shen, Central News (Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Reports State Minister Senzo Higai's statement that Japan will petition SCAP for improved police mobility and revision of the national-to-local police ratio as impoverished localities disband autonomous forces.
subfiles.title: Central News Dispatch on Need for Revising Police Law (FBIB Report)

subfiles.about: Reports a conversation with H. S. Eaton of SCAP G-2 Public Safety Division regarding proposed minor Police Law amendments, pistol distribution, and recent civil unrest.
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Summarizes G-2 police official H. S. Eaton's views opposing police recentralization, detailing proposed minor Police Law revisions, distribution of 14,000 American pistols, and police response to the Taira, Mitaka, and Shimoyama incidents.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 529: Views of Headquarters Police Official in Regard to Police Situation in Japan

subfiles.about: Reports on the political fallout from false press stories alleging SCAP rejected Prime Minister Yoshida's police reorganization and details friction between Cabinet and Government Section.
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Reports on false press claims of a SCAP rebuff to Prime Minister Yoshida, detailing Government Section's behind-the-scenes warnings against recentralization and the growing conflict between Cabinet authority and the National Public Safety Commission.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 528: Press Report Alleging Headquarters Communication to Prime Minister Regarding Proposed Police Reorganization

subfiles.about: Reports that SCAP rejected feelers from Prime Minister Yoshida seeking approval for a special police force and warned against relaxing purges.
subfiles.from: John Rich, International News Service
subfiles.summary: Reports that SCAP rejected Prime Minister Yoshida's feelers for a special police force, warning that the extreme right remained dangerous and opposing relaxation of political purges.
subfiles.title: Nippon Times Article: 'Special' Police Setup Said Rejected by SCAP (Enclosure No. 1 to Despatch No. 528)

subfiles.about: Investigates the origin of fabricated press reports alleging an exchange of correspondence between MacArthur and Yoshida on police reorganization.
subfiles.from: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Katsumi Ohno)
subfiles.summary: Evaluates the origin of leaked news stories alleging MacArthur rejected Yoshida's police plans, attributing leaks to journalist Norman Soong and political maneuvering by opposition parties or lower-echelon GHQ officials.
subfiles.title: Japanese Foreign Office Account of Background of Alleged MacArthur-Yoshida Correspondence (Enclosure No. 2 to Despatch No. 528)

subfiles.about: Prime Minister Yoshida denies foreign press reports alleging an exchange of letters with Allied Headquarters regarding a special police force.
subfiles.from: Prime Minister Shigeru Yoshida
subfiles.summary: Prime Minister Shigeru Yoshida categorically denies press reports alleging an exchange of letters with General MacArthur concerning the creation of a special police force, reaffirming full cooperation with SCAP.
subfiles.title: Statement of Prime Minister Shigeru Yoshida Denying Reports on Special Police (Enclosure No. 3 to Despatch No. 528)

subfiles.about: Reports statements by Yoshida and SCAP's Government Section denying reports of correspondence on a special police force, while Masuda affirms plans to revise the Police Law.
subfiles.from: Rutherford Poats, United Press / Nippon Times
subfiles.summary: Details denials by Prime Minister Yoshida and Government Section Deputy Chief Frank Rizzo of reported letters regarding a special police force, while Cabinet Secretary Masuda confirms plans to revise the Police Law.
subfiles.title: Nippon Times Article: GHQ and Premier Brand as Untrue Report in Papers (Enclosure No. 4 to Despatch No. 528)

subfiles.about: Summarizes a twelve-point police revision draft by the Democratic-Liberal Party expanding National Rural Police powers, creating an armed Keibitai, and subordinating police to the Cabinet.
subfiles.from: Nippon Keizai Shimbun (translated by Ministry of Foreign Affairs)
subfiles.summary: Details a twelve-point police revision proposal by the Democratic-Liberal Party, expanding National Rural Police powers over state crimes, creating a 30,000-man armed Keibitai, incorporating the Metropolitan Police Board, and subordinating police leadership to the Cabinet.
subfiles.title: Translation of Nippon Keizai Shimbun Article: Draft Outline of Plan for Revision of the Police System as Proposed by the Democratic-Liberal Party (Enclosure No. 5 to Despatch No. 528)

subfiles.about: Presents Prime Minister Yoshida's confidential argument for direct Cabinet control over the police and criticizing the political bias of the National Public Safety Commission.
subfiles.from: Prime Minister Shigeru Yoshida (delivered and translated by Katsumi Ohno)
subfiles.summary: Prime Minister Yoshida contends that the Cabinet must hold ultimate responsibility for public order, criticizing the National Public Safety Commission for obstructive, partisan attitudes stemming from its Katayama-era socialist appointees and urging immediate police reform.
subfiles.title: Prime Minister Yoshida's Statement to Mr. Sebald on Police Administration and the National Public Safety Commission (Enclosure No. 6 to Despatch No. 528)
subfiles.to: William J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan

subfiles.about: Lists the names, remaining terms of office, and professional backgrounds of the members of the National Public Safety Commission.
subfiles.from: Ministry of Foreign Affairs / USPOLAD
subfiles.summary: Lists the five members of the National Public Safety Commission, including their professions and remaining terms of office.
subfiles.title: List of the Members of the National Public Safety Commission (Enclosure No. 7 to Despatch No. 528)

subfiles.about: Summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 529 regarding Eaton's statements on minor Police Law revisions, police size limits, and improved civil order.
subfiles.from: Marshall Green, Division of Northeast Asian Affairs
subfiles.summary: Summarizes Despatch 529 regarding G-2 official Eaton's statements on proposed minor Police Law amendments and recent abatement of disorders.
subfiles.title: Department of State Memorandum on Tokyo's Despatch No. 529 Concerning Police Situation

subfiles.about: Summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 528 regarding the INS article, SCAP's position, and Prime Minister Yoshida's conflict with General Whitney over police control.
subfiles.from: Marshall Green, Division of Northeast Asian Affairs
subfiles.summary: Summarizes Despatch 528 concerning the INS leak, Government Section attitudes, and Yoshida's dispute with Whitney over Cabinet police control.
subfiles.title: Department of State Memorandum on Tokyo's Despatch No. 528 Concerning Police Controversy

subfiles.about: Transmits a State Department memorandum on the Japanese police establishment to Assistant Secretary Voorhees for his trip to Japan.
subfiles.from: W. Walton Butterworth, Director for Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Forwards a memorandum supplementing NSC 13/3 progress reports to Assistant Secretary of the Army Voorhees for his upcoming trip to Japan, urging discussions with General MacArthur on Japanese police legislation.
subfiles.title: Letter from W. Walton Butterworth to Tracy S. Voorhees Transmitting Memorandum on Japanese Police Establishment
subfiles.to: Tracy S. Voorhees, Assistant Secretary of the Army

subfiles.about: Critiques SCAP G-2's complacency regarding Japanese internal security and advocates broadening national police powers under NSC 13/3 in light of widespread sabotage and communist unrest.
subfiles.from: Marshall Green, Division of Northeast Asian Affairs
subfiles.summary: Criticizes SCAP G-2's opposition to police expansion under NSC 13/3, citing over 750 sabotage cases, the Taira station seizure, and vigilante groups, and advocates broadening national police powers to ensure internal security without reviving a police state.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on the Japanese Police Establishment
subfiles.to: Tracy S. Voorhees, Assistant Secretary of the Army

subfiles.about: Transmits copies of correspondence between Prime Minister Yoshida and General MacArthur concerning Police Law revision and police centralization.
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Transmits letters exchanged between Prime Minister Yoshida and General MacArthur regarding police coordination, noting MacArthur's rejection of centralization and Japanese officials' continuing efforts to amend the police system.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 610: Yoshida-MacArthur Correspondence on Police Law

subfiles.about: Appeals to General MacArthur for advice on revising the Police Law to bring police units under unified control and closer Cabinet liaison.
subfiles.from: Prime Minister Shigeru Yoshida
subfiles.summary: Prime Minister Yoshida expresses deep concern over police fragmentation and isolation during recent unrest, citing the Mitaka train incident and requesting General MacArthur's advice on unifying police control under government liaison.
subfiles.title: Letter from Prime Minister Shigeru Yoshida to General Douglas MacArthur on Police Coordination (Enclosure No. 1 to Despatch No. 610)
subfiles.to: General Douglas MacArthur, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers

subfiles.about: Rejects Prime Minister Yoshida's request for police recentralization, citing ongoing improvements in training and arms loans and defending the public safety commission system.
subfiles.from: General Douglas MacArthur, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.summary: General MacArthur rejects Prime Minister Yoshida's appeal for police centralization, reporting substantial gains in training and handgun distribution, and insisting that coordination problems require educational development rather than structural changes to the Police Law.
subfiles.title: Letter from General Douglas MacArthur to Prime Minister Shigeru Yoshida Reaffirming Police Decentralization (Enclosure No. 2 to Despatch No. 610)

subfiles.about: Sets forth SCAP's foundational directive on police decentralization, autonomous municipal police forces, civilian public safety commissions, and the creation of an Attorney General's Office.
subfiles.from: General Douglas MacArthur, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.summary: General MacArthur outlines fundamental principles for reforming Japan's police, approving a 125,000-man limit and National Rural Police, mandating municipal decentralization under civilian public safety commissions, and recommending the creation of an Attorney General's Office.
subfiles.title: Letter from General Douglas MacArthur to Prime Minister Tetsu Katayama on Reorganization of the Japanese Police System (Enclosure No. 3 to Despatch No. 610)
